segments.original: Our story begins with a man waking up in a bathtub. In the dark, he wakes in a panic, stretching out his arms to find something to hold on to. He hears a voice in front of him, and suddenly the lights come on. The man finds himself in a decrepit bathroom, chained to the wall like the man across from him, with a corpse on the floor between them. So begins the journey into one of the biggest horror franchises, Saw. Since its U.S. release on October 29, 2004, the franchise has gained a loyal fan base. For many horror fans, Saw is what The Evil Dead (1981), A Nightmare on Elm Street (1984) or Friday the 13th (1980) was to horror in the 1980s. What drew so many fans was the gore, the torture and the imaginative "games" that the villain Jigsaw would devise. Saw is a film that began with a small idea, and while the sequels reshaped that original idea by adding new elements, the original remains the high point of the saga. By combining unique story, visual and violent ideas on a small budget, Saw would become one of the most important horror films of the new century.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Saw is the brainchild of James Wan (b. 1977) and Leigh Whannell (b. 1977). The two friends shared a love of cinema and wanted to write and finance their own film. One of the original inspirations for Saw actually came from The Blair Witch Project (1999); both Wan and Whannell realized that a film didn't need much money to be truly scary. The two saved enough to put together a short version of the project and eventually found distribution backing through Lionsgate. Driven by the urge to make a film and the mindset of keeping it affordable, they realized the best way to do it was to make the film in a condensed form. By focusing the main story on just two men in a room, they could save on the budget while still telling the story. These budget constraints also applied to the actual look of the picture. Wan originally wanted Saw to have a "Hitchcockian" style, but because of the limited shooting time they could afford, not every scene could be planned the ideal way. Yet this is what made possible the rough, gritty camerawork of Saw, helping to bring an atmosphere of grime and dread to every scene. That atmosphere is a hugely important part of Saw.

segments.original: Originally called "splatter films," torture porn is a horror subgenre that incorporates themes of excessive violence, gore, nudity, mutilation, torture and sadism. Earlier films that would fit these themes include Dawn of the Dead (1978), The Evil Dead and Dead Alive (1992). An important note to keep in mind about these earlier works (especially the last two) is that the violence was used in a comic sense, meaning the violence and gore were steeped in black humor. It would be the dawn of the 2000s that saw the resurgence of this subgenre, and where we would transition from "splatter films" to "torture porn" (the shift becoming far more sinister and horrific). The two main players in this resurgence would be Eli Roth's (b. 1972) Hostel (2006) and Saw. These films portrayed their violence through extreme visual measures, including new and more terrible kinds of violent acts that we would see on screen, using the camera to force us to watch such violence.

segments.original: Wan and Whannell never intended Saw to be a torture porn film. Even though the gore of the traps is the selling point of each Saw sequel, the original film was meant to be a horror mystery with torture scenes. Even if that wasn't their intention, the film was one of the main kicks that launched the popularity of torture porn films. It is partly thanks to Saw that we, as an audience, began to accept more violence in our cinema. Of course there were gruesome horror films before Saw, but the way it and Hostel portrayed violence (not to mention the profits of both) helped encourage studios to push for more works in that style.

segments.original: The first truly significant example of found footage can be found in Cannibal Holocaust (1980), an Italian film whose screenplay centers on the rescue of a group of American filmmakers lost in the Amazon rainforest. Anthropologist Harold Monroe (Robert Kerman) is in charge of the rescue and documents everything on video.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: But the genre gained greater prominence with the release of The Blair Witch Project in 1999. It opens with an introductory text saying that 3 film students disappeared in a forest in October 1994 while shooting a documentary. A year later, their footage was found by an anthropology student. This footage had supposedly been handed over to the police and used as evidence. The police, believing the footage was a hoax, released the films for public viewing. The viewer is then taken through what would have been the students' "witch hunt." There are "six days" of footage, and when the footage ends there is only silence. Made on a very small budget, The Blair Witch Project became a hit with mainstream audiences. People debated it, and the less informed speculated about whether or not it was real. Many disputed the police's opinion, insisting that this footage could not be a "hoax." Little by little, word spread that The Blair Witch Project was a professional production meant to pass as homemade. The Blair Witch Project got a Hollywood-style sequel that never took off.

segments.original: Almost ten years later, there was a surge of releases in the genre: Paranormal Activity and [REC] were the big names of 2007. The following year came Quarantine (2008) and Cloverfield (2008). Of the four titles, the most significant in terms of box-office success was Paranormal Activity. One of its standout features is that, like The Blair Witch Project, it relies very little on visual effects: its horror is psychological. As psychologists say, human beings are far more afraid of what they cannot see. The imagination is always more compelling than any concrete image. Some films are not pure found footage but apply the same techniques of psychological horror and naturalistic acting. A good example of a hybrid film is The Fourth Kind (2009), starring Milla Jovovich (b. 1975). Here, the production is a blend: there is found footage, but it is part of a staged game, intercut with reenactments by well-known professional actors.

segments.original: The film opens with Milla speaking to the camera, introducing herself as an actress, as well as the character she will play, Dr. Abigail Tyler. She also states that the film is a dramatization of events that took place from October 1 to 9, 2000. She then explains that, to help the viewer better understand the events of the story, the director has included archival footage from Dr. Abigail's psychologist, who personally documented more than 65 hours of video and audio material. Milla's statement creates an atmosphere of psychological tension and great realism. The film then unfolds in a context of doubt, suspense and terror. The found footage element complements the horror of the plot, adding a dose of realism and making the viewer (lacking any extra information during the film) afraid of alien abduction.

segments.original: Generally, horror films have high budgets because special effects are expensive. In the case of found footage, these films enjoy a certain "poetic license": in theory, the actors are the ones filming, and the images always lean toward a more homemade style, so there is no great need to spend money on such effects. In the case of Paranormal Activity, the production cost was around 10,000 dollars, a pittance.
